posts.title: AI doesn't replace jobs. It takes over tasks.
posts.cta: Comment: Which task would you hand off first?

instagram.caption:
AI won't take your job. It takes tasks off your plate.

Every role is a bundle of tasks. Some repeat every week. Others need judgment, trust and responsibility.

The first kind can often be automated. The second stays with people.

Which task would you hand off first in your team?

linkedin.caption:
“Which jobs will AI replace?” is the wrong question for business owners.

A more useful one: Which tasks in my team repeat every week and need no judgment?

An office manager answers emails, books travel, chases invoices, orders supplies and settles disputes. Part of that follows fixed steps. The rest needs experience and responsibility.

That's why the same role can shrink in one company and grow in another. It depends on which tasks get automated and what happens with the time that frees up.

My suggestion: take one role and break it down into 10 to 15 tasks. The candidates will jump out at you.

Which task would you hand off first?

posts.title: Automation, AI workflow or AI agent? One question is enough.
posts.cta: Save it for the next tool discussion

instagram.caption:
Automation, AI workflow, AI agent. Three terms that get mixed up constantly.

All three run without you starting each step. The difference comes down to one question: Who decides the next step?

The rules → automation
The rules, with AI helping in one step → AI workflow
The AI itself → AI agent

Save this for the next time someone says “we need an agent”.

linkedin.caption:
“We need an AI agent.” I hear it a lot. Usually something else is meant.

Automations, AI workflows and AI agents all run without someone starting each step. What sets them apart: who decides the path.

• Automation: fixed rules, same path every time. Reliable, fast, cheap, easy to check. Breaks on anything it wasn't told about.
• AI workflow: fixed path, one step asks an AI. Handles messy text and documents, but the AI step needs a check.
• AI agent: gets a goal and picks its own steps. Adapts to the unplanned, but is harder to predict and to check.

The difference decides what you build, what it costs and how far you can trust it.

In practice, most useful business work sits in the first two.

Which of the three are you already using?

One test that saves me a lot of time in conversations about AI agents:

Can you write the steps down on a sheet of paper?

If yes, you don't need an agent. An automation with fixed rules will do. If the input is messy, like free-form emails or scans, add an AI step. The path still stays fixed.

An agent only makes sense when the path really can't be planned in advance. And then with limits: which tools it may use, what it may change and where a person has to approve.

posts.title: Is it worth automating? The five-question test
posts.cta: Save it and run it on a real process at your next team meeting

instagram.caption:
Not every process should be automated.

Five questions, each yes or no:
1 Does it happen at least once a week?
2 Does it follow the same steps most of the time?
3 Does a person copy, sort or retype information?
4 Is the input digital, or easy to make digital?
5 Can a mistake be fixed, or checked by a person before it matters?

Four or more yes answers: worth a closer look. Three scored examples are in the carousel.

Save the test for your next process.

linkedin.caption:
Before you talk about tools, test the process.

I use a simple test with five yes/no questions:

1. Does it happen at least once a week?
2. Does it follow the same steps most of the time?
3. Does a person copy, sort or retype information?
4. Is the input digital, or easy to make digital (email, form, PDF, photo)?
5. Can a mistake be fixed, or checked by a person before it matters?

Four or five yes answers: take a closer look.

Three examples:
• Typing vendor bills into the accounting system: 5/5
• Negotiating a supplier contract: 0/5
• Replying to the same ten customer questions: 4/5, but keep an approval step, because wrong answers can upset customers.

Start with a process that scores 4 or 5. A clear, boring win does more than an impressive project that never ships.

Which process in your business would score 5 out of 5?

Businesses rarely lose time in one big place. It leaks away in many small ones.

Six patterns that show up in almost every SME:

posts.title: Before you automate: the 7 fields of a process map
posts.cta: Save it for your next process

instagram.caption:
Before any tool comes into play, every process needs a one-page description.

Seven fields are enough:
Trigger · Input · Steps · Decisions · Exceptions · Output · Owner & volume

Important: fill them in with the person who does the work. They know the exceptions. You don't.

Save the 7 fields for your next process.

linkedin.caption:
Most failed automations fail in the description, not in the tooling.

If you can't explain a process to a new colleague in five minutes, a tool can't run it either.

That's why I describe every process with the same seven fields:

1. Trigger: What starts the process?
2. Input: What information comes in?
3. Steps: What happens, in order?
4. Decisions: Where does it branch?
5. Exceptions: What goes wrong?
6. Output: What is the result?
7. Owner and volume: Who is responsible, and how often does it run?

Take vendor bills: a bill arrives by email or on paper. Vendor, date, item codes, cost, quantity. Compare with the order. Exceptions: handwriting, missing date, a vendor not in the system.

Most important: fill in the fields with the person who does the work, not for them.

Which field is missing most often in your process descriptions?

Before I suggest any solution, I calculate what a process costs today.

The formula is simple:
minutes per run × runs per week × 52 ÷ 60 = hours per year

An example: 8 minutes × 40 runs per week × 52 ÷ 60 = about 277 hours per year.

Two things matter:

posts.title: Map a process on one page
posts.cta: Save

linkedin.caption:
A picture exposes gaps that text hides.

Process people draw in a standard called BPMN. You don't need the whole standard. Six elements cover almost everything:

• Trigger: what starts the process
• Action: one step a person or a system carries out
• Decision: a question with two or more ways out
• End: the process is finished (there can be more than one)
• Lane: one row per owner
• Pool: the frame around the whole process

The carousel shows a vendor bill drawn with two lanes: system and purchasing.

Two things I look at first when reading a diagram:
1. If a step doesn't fit into any lane, nobody owns it yet.
2. Every arrow that crosses a lane line is a handoff. That's where processes usually stall.

Do you draw your processes before you automate them?

posts.title: What a workflow tool can do, and what it can't
posts.cta: Follow for more practical examples

linkedin.caption:
A workflow tool like n8n or Make doesn't run your business. It carries out single steps, in the order you set.

I like to describe it as a very fast, very literal assistant: it does exactly what the map says. Every time. And nothing else.

What it can do:
• Four actions on data: read, add, update, delete
• Logic in between: if/else, filters, loops, waits, error handling
• Start on its own: when a form arrives, on a schedule, or when a row changes

What it can't do:
• Know your process
• Guess when a case isn't described
• Judge without an AI step (and with one, it can be wrong)
• Reach apps that aren't connected
• Look after itself when fields change or a login expires

Deciding what to build and what happens in unusual cases stays with you.

posts.title: Let AI prepare. Let a person approve.
posts.cta: Save it for your next workflow

instagram.caption:
The most reliable rule for AI in business: let AI prepare, let a person approve.

Three places where a person almost always belongs:
→ before money moves
→ before anything goes to a customer
→ whenever the AI is unsure

That doesn't slow you down. It makes sure a mistake gets caught before it does damage.

Save the three places for your next workflow.

linkedin.caption:
“Can't the AI just do it on its own?”

Sometimes, yes. For critical steps, no.

AI can be wrong, and it can be wrong with full confidence. That's normal and won't go away completely. So every first version I build has a human check before anything irreversible happens.

The principle: AI proposes, a person approves, the system acts.

Three places where a person almost always belongs:
• before money moves
• before anything goes to a customer
• whenever the AI is unsure

Take vendor bills: AI reads the bill. If it matches the order, purchasing just checks and approves. If it doesn't, they correct the data first. Only then does the system create the order.

Rule of thumb: a person belongs wherever a mistake is expensive or hard to undo.

Where does the approval sit in your processes?

linkedin.caption:
An automation runs without you. That's the point. And that's exactly why we clarify upfront what happens when it gets something wrong.

My risk check before every build has four questions:

1. What happens if the AI is wrong? That decides whether a person needs to check, and how strictly.
2. Does it touch personal or customer data? Then privacy rules apply. Ask the company which AI services it may use before sending anything.
3. Who is notified when it fails? Silent failures are the worst kind. Every failure needs a name next to it.
4. Can it be switched off quickly? You always need a stop button, and the owner needs to know where it is.

None of these questions is technical. All of them decide whether an automation deserves trust.

posts.title: It works in testing. That's not enough.
posts.cta: Follow

linkedin.caption:
The most common sentence right before the first trouble: “It worked in testing.”

A workflow that works on your example won't necessarily work on real data. Real life brings missing information, odd formatting, handwriting, a different language.

My rule: ten real examples, at least three of them ugly.

Then four check questions:
1. Does it produce the right result on the clean cases?
2. What does it do on the ugly cases? It should pass them to a person, not guess.
3. Does anybody get notified when it fails?
4. Is the time saved close to the estimate?

And after a week in production, look again: check the results, compare the time saved, ask users what annoys them.

Exceptions decide whether an automation works in day-to-day business.

1 Before you start
2 While you build
3 Before handover

linkedin.caption:
A checklist I go through for every automation, from a small internal workflow to a client project.

Before you start: Does the process happen at least weekly? Is it described with the seven fields? Does the person who does the work agree with the map? Is it clear what happens when it fails, and who finds out?

While you build: smallest version first. Approval before anything irreversible. Exceptions go to a person instead of being guessed. Ten real examples, including ugly ones. Personal data handled according to company rules.

Before handover: one-page description, a known stop button, failure alerts to a real person, scope written down and agreed.

After it's live: check results after one week, compare the time saved with the estimate, ask users what annoys them.
